title: Big questions
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: The module's system is one suffix with two shapes. -tā makes a FEMININE abstract and -tva a NEUTER one, they mean the same thing, and both attach to a stem the learner already owns: mitram gives mitratā, and the same machinery gives svatantratā and mahattvam. The suffix's only job is to turn a quality into a thing.

WHICH SUFFIX IS NOT A FREE CHOICE HERE, AND THE REASON IS THIS COURSE'S OWN INDEX. L2-M3 wrote its adjectives in the masculine and the neuter, so the feminine adjective stock on the whole ladder is a handful of rows and there is no feminine uttamam, no feminine hrasvam and no feminine colour at all. So an abstract that will take an adjective is opened in -tva — mahattvam uttamam is writable — and -tā is used where the noun is the subject of asti or rocate, or an object.

A DERIVATIVE IS NOT A SHAPE. mitratā is its own row and not a form of L2-M2's mitram, so a tap on it lands on a note about friendship and not on a note about a friend. mahattvam is the same: the consonant stem inside it appears there and nowhere else, with its internal doubling written in full, and no cell of its declension is opened by it.

Every abstract in this module is written as a SUBJECT and never predicated onto something else: mitratā mahyam rocate, svatantratā asti. That is not a style rule — it is the gender law of the line above, and it is what keeps an adjective away from a word that has no shape to give it.

English builds its abstracts off VERBS and hears them as actions: freedom, belief, understanding. These are built off adjectives and nouns, and the suffix does nothing but make a quality into a thing. So learn each one on a stem you already own — mitram to mitratā — rather than as a new class of word.

English abstract talk leans on a copula this course does not write. aham chātraḥ has no verb and never did, so jīvanam sundaram is a complete sentence, and the commonest error in this module is bolting asti onto a line that was already finished. The other half of the rule, from L1-M3 and unchanged: the present copula is optional, but na asti is not.

praśnaḥ is the question as a thing and viśvāsaḥ is the belief, and both are masculine. A whole question is carried into a sentence by L3-M5's iti: jīvanam kim asti iti mama praśnaḥ asti is 'my question is what life is', and without the iti the two halves would collide.

What is GOOD is said with L4-M4's hitam and L3-M6's sukham, and with nothing else. mūlyam is L1-M8's and it is owned as a PRICE; its moral reading — a value in the sense this module's job line means — is written nowhere on this course, for the fifth time after api, vā, yat and phalam. L3-M3's satyam is the agreement word, 'true, that's right', so it is not pressed into service here as a noun meaning truth either.

dharmaḥ is named in English and written in no row of this course. The reason is honesty rather than the index: no one-line gloss of it is true, and a row's cue is one line. A learner who wants it wants a paragraph, and a paragraph is not what a word row is.

STILL WRITTEN NOWHERE, and named here because this is the module that would otherwise reach for them. mahat in any declined cell — mahattvam routes around it, with the consonant stem sealed inside one token, exactly as L4-M9's mahānagaram did. And asmi, so the course reaches its last level having never written the first-person present of the verb to be, because aham chātraḥ has never needed one.

sentences.display: jīvanam kim asti iti mama praśnaḥ asti.
sentences.script: जीवनम् किम् अस्ति इति मम प्रश्नः अस्ति।
sentences.cue: My question is what life is.
sentences.literal: life what is thus of-me question is

words.note: Life, a neuter noun — the whole of it rather than a lifetime or a living. It is the subject of most of this module and it takes a neuter word beside it.
L1-M2's kim, and here it is 'what' rather than the yes/no marker: it stands where the answer would stand, which is the placement rule that sorts its two jobs.
L1-M3's copula. With an 'of me' in front of it, it is the whole of 'have': mama praśnaḥ asti.
L3-M5's quotative. It is what carries a whole question or claim into a sentence as a single thing instead of interrupting it.
L1-M1's 'of me'. In mama mate it owns the opinion; everywhere else in this module it owns the question.
The question as a THING, masculine — something a person HAS rather than something they do. mama praśnaḥ asti is 'I have a question'.
The second asti belongs to the outer sentence. mama praśnaḥ asti is 'I have a question', which is the same have-frame L1-M3 opened.

sentences.trap: There are two astis in this line and they belong to different sentences. The first is inside the question; iti closes it; the second is the verb of the sentence that HAS the question.
sentences.sound: JEE-va-nam KIM AS-ti i-ti MA-ma PRASH-nah AS-ti. The śn of praśnaḥ is the palatal sibilant followed by the dental n, not the retroflex ṣ. Said at speed praśnaḥ asti joins as praśno asti, the visarga turning to o in front of the vowel.

variations.display: jīvanam kim asti iti bhavataḥ praśnaḥ asti.
variations.script: जीवनम् किम् अस्ति इति भवतः प्रश्नः अस्ति।
variations.cue: Your question is what life is.
variations.changed: the question is handed to the listener, and only the possessor changes

variations.display: jīvanam kim asti iti saḥ pṛcchati.
variations.script: जीवनम् किम् अस्ति इति सः पृच्छति।
variations.cue: He asks what life is.
variations.changed: somebody else asks it out loud, which is the blunter form the question usually takes

variations.display: mama praśnaḥ asti.
variations.script: मम प्रश्नः अस्ति।
variations.cue: I have a question.
variations.changed: the quoted half falls away, leaving the frame that every question in this module is hung on

mistake.display: jīvanam kim asti mama praśnaḥ asti.
mistake.why: Without iti the two clauses collide and the line has two verbs and no join. iti is what turns a whole question into one thing that the outer sentence can be about.

sentences.usage: The module's opening move, and the shape worth copying: put the big question inside iti and then say what it is to you. Asked bare, jīvanam kim asti is a challenge; wrapped like this, it is an admission.
sentences.mnemonic: Wrap the question, then own it.

sentences.display: mitratā mahyam rocate, yataḥ mitratā sukham dadāti.
sentences.script: मित्रता मह्यम् रोचते, यतः मित्रता सुखम् ददाति।
sentences.cue: I value friendship, because friendship gives happiness.
sentences.literal: friendship to-me is-pleasing, because friendship happiness gives

words.note: Friendship. It is built from L2-M2's mitram with the -tā suffix and it is its OWN word, not a shape of it: the friend is neuter, the friendship is feminine.
L1-M1's 'to me'. rocate answers to the thing liked and never to the liker, so the person always stands in this shape.
L1-M1's 'is pleasing'. With an abstract noun in front of it, it is the ordinary way this course says a person values something.
L1-M9's 'because', opening its own half. It is the reason-giver this course has used since its first level and it needs nothing else around it.
L3-M6's happiness, neuter, and the thing given. It is lighter in this language than the English word is.
L5-M1's 'gives', third person. An abstract noun can be the giver here exactly as vidyā is in vidyā dadāti vinayam.

sentences.trap: The noun is repeated in the second half rather than replaced by a pronoun, and that is deliberate: sā is 'she, that woman' on this course, so a pronoun standing for mitratā would send a learner to a row about a person.
sentences.sound: mi-tra-TAA MAH-yam ROH-cha-tay, YA-tah mi-tra-TAA SU-kham da-DAA-ti. The c of rocate is the palatal 'ch' of church and never the k of cat. The -tā of mitratā is long and carries the weight of the word.

variations.display: mitratā mahyam rocate.
variations.script: मित्रता मह्यम् रोचते।
variations.cue: I value friendship.
variations.changed: the reason drops away, leaving the bare statement of value the module is built on

variations.display: mitratā bhavate rocate, yataḥ mitratā sukham dadāti.
variations.script: मित्रता भवते रोचते, यतः मित्रता सुखम् ददाति।
variations.cue: You value friendship, because friendship gives happiness.
variations.changed: the person who values forks to the listener, and the verb does not move because it never answered to them

variations.display: kim mitratā bhavate rocate?
variations.script: किम् मित्रता भवते रोचते?
variations.cue: Do you value friendship?
variations.changed: asked rather than asserted, which is how a conversation about values actually opens

mistake.display: mitratā mahyam rocati, yataḥ mitratā sukham dadāti.
mistake.why: rocate ends in -te and not in -ti. It belongs to the set L3-M3's manye belongs to, and the -ti ending was copied across from dadāti at the end of the line.

sentences.usage: How a value is stated and then grounded. rocate is the ordinary way this course says somebody values something, and the abstract noun sits in front of it as the subject exactly as a fruit or a book would.
sentences.mnemonic: Say the value, then say why.

sentences.display: mama mate svatantratā eva uttamam dhanam.
sentences.script: मम मते स्वतन्त्रता एव उत्तमम् धनम्।
sentences.cue: In my view freedom is the greatest wealth.
sentences.literal: of-me in-view freedom indeed excellent wealth

words.note: L1-M1's 'of me'. In mama mate it owns the opinion; everywhere else in this module it owns the question.
L4-M4's 'opinion' in its 'in' shape. mama mate is the whole idiom and it is how a claim about anything large is marked as a claim.
Freedom, built with the same -tā suffix and feminine like every -tā word. It is a quality made into a thing, which is all the suffix ever does.
L5-M1's emphasiser, standing AFTER the word it lifts. In front of it, it lifts nothing at all.
L2-M3's praise word, neuter here. It has no feminine shape anywhere on this course, which is the fact that decided which suffix each abstract in this module got.
L3-M8's wealth, neuter. The subject is feminine and the predicate neuter, and nothing is wrong with that: two different nouns need not share a gender to be equated.

sentences.trap: There is no verb in this sentence and none is missing. L1-M3's rule holds: the present copula is optional, so a claim of this size can be made with no verb at all.

variations.display: mama mate mitratā eva uttamam dhanam.
variations.script: मम मते मित्रता एव उत्तमम् धनम्।
variations.cue: In my view friendship is the greatest wealth.
variations.changed: the other abstract in the subject slot, which is the only slot either of them is written in

variations.display: svatantratā eva uttamam dhanam.
variations.script: स्वतन्त्रता एव उत्तमम् धनम्।
variations.cue: Freedom is the greatest wealth.
variations.changed: the hedge is dropped and the view becomes a pronouncement — one word shorter and much louder

variations.display: mama mate svatantratā eva uttamam dhanam, kintu mitratā api uttamam dhanam.
variations.script: मम मते स्वतन्त्रता एव उत्तमम् धनम्, किन्तु मित्रता अपि उत्तमम् धनम्।
variations.cue: In my view freedom is the greatest wealth, but friendship is too.
variations.changed: the claim is softened by a second one, which is what a speaker does when the first was too strong

sentences.usage: The claim shape of the module, and it is L5-M1's vidyā eva uttamam dhanam with a new subject. mama mate is what marks it as a view rather than a fact, and dropping it turns the line into an announcement.
sentences.mnemonic: mama mate turns a fact into a view.

sentences.display: mahattvam uttamam na asti, kintu hitam uttamam asti.
sentences.script: महत्त्वम् उत्तमम् न अस्ति, किन्तु हितम् उत्तमम् अस्ति।
sentences.cue: Greatness is not what is best; what does good is.
sentences.literal: greatness excellent not is, but the-beneficial excellent is

words.note: Greatness, built with -tva instead and therefore NEUTER. That is the whole reason it was chosen: a neuter abstract can take uttamam, adhikam and alpam, and a feminine one cannot on this ladder.
L2-M3's praise word, neuter here. It has no feminine shape anywhere on this course, which is the fact that decided which suffix each abstract in this module got.
L1-M2's negation, standing in front of the verb it denies. na asti is the whole of 'is not'.
L1-M3's copula. With an 'of me' in front of it, it is the whole of 'have': mama praśnaḥ asti.
L1-M10's 'but', opening its half. The sentence refuses one thing and then names another, which is what a values claim usually has to do.
L4-M4's 'good for somebody', as against L2-M3's uttamam, which simply praises. It is the word an argument holds its ground with.

sentences.trap: This sentence is the reason mahattvam was built with -tva and not with -tā. uttamam has no feminine shape anywhere on this ladder, so the same claim about a -tā abstract could not be written at all.
sentences.sound: ma-HAT-tvam UT-ta-mam na AS-ti, KIN-tu HI-tam UT-ta-mam AS-ti. The tt of mahattvam is a held double t and the tv after it is one cluster, so the middle of the word is 'hat-tvam' and not 'ha-tat-vam'. Said at speed na asti runs together as nāsti.

variations.display: mahattvam uttamam na asti.
variations.script: महत्त्वम् उत्तमम् न अस्ति।
variations.cue: Greatness is not what is best.
variations.changed: the refusal stands alone, which is blunter and leaves the listener to supply the second half

variations.display: mahattvam uttamam na, hitam uttamam.
variations.script: महत्त्वम् उत्तमम् न, हितम् उत्तमम्।
variations.cue: Greatness, not best; what does good, best.
variations.changed: both copulas dropped, and the line reads as the maxim it is trying to be

variations.display: kim mahattvam uttamam asti?
variations.script: किम् महत्त्वम् उत्तमम् अस्ति?
variations.cue: Is greatness what is best?
variations.changed: asked rather than refused, which is how the question is put to somebody who thinks it is

mistake.display: mitratā uttamā na asti, kintu hitam uttamam asti.
mistake.why: uttamā is not a word this course has ever written: L2-M3 taught uttamaḥ and uttamam and no feminine at all. That gap is exactly why the module built its predicated abstract with -tva, and why the -tā abstracts are never given an adjective.

sentences.usage: The module's one sharp claim, and it is made entirely out of neuter words so that the adjective has somewhere to land. Both halves use the same praise word, which is what makes the refusal in the first half land.

sentences.cue: My belief is that life is beautiful.

words.note: Life, a neuter noun — the whole of it rather than a lifetime or a living. It is the subject of most of this module and it takes a neuter word beside it.
L1-M9's 'beautiful', neuter beside jīvanam. The quoted half has no copula at all, which is L1-M3's rule holding inside a quotation as well as outside one.
L3-M5's quotative. It is what carries a whole question or claim into a sentence as a single thing instead of interrupting it.
L1-M1's 'of me'. In mama mate it owns the opinion; everywhere else in this module it owns the question.
The belief, masculine — a thing a person HAS rather than something they do. It covers trust in a person as well as belief in a claim.

sentences.trap: Neither half has a verb. The quoted claim is verbless and so is the frame around it, and the whole sentence is five words with nothing finite in it.

variations.display: jīvanam sundaram iti bhavataḥ viśvāsaḥ.
variations.script: जीवनम् सुन्दरम् इति भवतः विश्वासः।
variations.cue: Your belief is that life is beautiful.
variations.changed: the belief is attributed to the listener, which is how it is repeated back in a disagreement

variations.display: jīvanam sundaram iti mama viśvāsaḥ asti.
variations.script: जीवनम् सुन्दरम् इति मम विश्वासः अस्ति।
variations.cue: My belief is that life is beautiful.
variations.changed: the copula is written out, which is heavier and slightly more insistent

variations.display: jīvanam sundaram iti aham manye.
variations.script: जीवनम् सुन्दरम् इति अहम् मन्ये।
variations.cue: I think life is beautiful.
variations.changed: L3-M3's manye replaces the noun frame, which softens a belief into an opinion

sentences.usage: How a belief is stated without arguing for it. Anything quoted with iti and handed to viśvāsaḥ is marked as the speaker's own, which is the politest way this course has of saying something large.
sentences.mnemonic: Quote the claim, then own it as yours.

sentences.display: mama ekaḥ praśnaḥ asti, kintu aham na jānāmi.
sentences.script: मम एकः प्रश्नः अस्ति, किन्तु अहम् न जानामि।
sentences.cue: I have one question, but I do not know.
sentences.literal: of-me one question is, but I not I-know

words.note: L1-M1's 'of me'. In mama mate it owns the opinion; everywhere else in this module it owns the question.
L1-M8's 'one' in its masculine shape, because praśnaḥ is masculine. The ending is copied from the noun and never chosen.
The question as a THING, masculine — something a person HAS rather than something they do. mama praśnaḥ asti is 'I have a question'.
L1-M3's copula. With an 'of me' in front of it, it is the whole of 'have': mama praśnaḥ asti.
'But', opening its half. The turn here is from having a question to not having an answer, which is the whole of the sentence.
L1-M1's 'I', written out because the second half changes who the sentence is about.
The negation in front of its verb.
L2-M8's 'I know', in the first person because the speaker is the one not knowing. Its row is displayed in this shape, which is the shape this sentence needs.

sentences.trap: ekaḥ and not ekam: praśnaḥ is masculine. The numeral has three endings and copies whichever noun it stands beside, which is the same fact L1-M8 taught with fruit and flowers.

variations.display: mama ekaḥ praśnaḥ asti, kintu mama viśvāsaḥ api asti.
variations.script: मम एकः प्रश्नः अस्ति, किन्तु मम विश्वासः अपि अस्ति।
variations.cue: I have one question, but I have a belief too.
variations.changed: the admission is balanced by something the speaker does have, which is the module's steadiest posture

variations.display: mama ekaḥ praśnaḥ asti.
variations.script: मम एकः प्रश्नः अस्ति।
variations.cue: I have one question.
variations.changed: the second half drops and the line becomes the ordinary opening of a conversation

variations.display: kim bhavataḥ api ekaḥ praśnaḥ asti?
variations.script: किम् भवतः अपि एकः प्रश्नः अस्ति?
variations.cue: Do you have a question too?
variations.changed: turned outward as a question to the listener, which is how the subject gets passed on

sentences.usage: The honest posture of the whole module. A question owned and an answer not claimed is a stronger position in this register than an answer asserted, and it is the shape most of these sentences end in.
sentences.mnemonic: Own the question, not the answer.

sentences.display: svatantratā mahyam rocate, kintu mitratā adhikam rocate.
sentences.script: स्वतन्त्रता मह्यम् रोचते, किन्तु मित्रता अधिकम् रोचते।
sentences.cue: I value freedom, but I value friendship more.
sentences.literal: freedom to-me is-pleasing, but friendship more is-pleasing

words.note: Freedom, built with the same -tā suffix and feminine like every -tā word. It is a quality made into a thing, which is all the suffix ever does.
L1-M1's 'to me'. rocate answers to the thing liked and never to the liker, so the person always stands in this shape.
L1-M1's 'is pleasing'. With an abstract noun in front of it, it is the ordinary way this course says a person values something.
'But', opening the half that outranks the first. A preference in this course is built out of two statements and not out of a comparative word.
Friendship. It is built from L2-M2's mitram with the -tā suffix and it is its OWN word, not a shape of it: the friend is neuter, the friendship is feminine.
L2-M9's 'more', standing in front of the verb and saying more OF the pleasing. There is no word for 'than' anywhere in this sentence and none is needed.

sentences.trap: There is no comparative adjective in this line. adhikam raises the VERB — more pleasing — which is the only comparison machinery this course has ever written.
sentences.sound: sva-tan-tra-TAA MAH-yam ROH-cha-tay, KIN-tu mi-tra-TAA A-dhi-kam ROH-cha-tay. svatantratā opens on the same sv cluster as svasti and carries four light syllables before its long ending. Said at speed mitratā adhikam runs on as mitratādhikam, the two a-sounds fusing into one long one.

variations.display: mitratā mahyam rocate, kintu svatantratā adhikam rocate.
variations.script: मित्रता मह्यम् रोचते, किन्तु स्वतन्त्रता अधिकम् रोचते।
variations.cue: I value friendship, but I value freedom more.
variations.changed: the ranking is reversed, and nothing else in the line moves

variations.display: svatantratā mahyam rocate, mitratā api mahyam rocate.
variations.script: स्वतन्त्रता मह्यम् रोचते, मित्रता अपि मह्यम् रोचते।
variations.cue: I value freedom, and I value friendship too.
variations.changed: api replaces adhikam, so the two are levelled instead of ranked

variations.display: svatantratā mahyam alpam rocate, kintu mitratā adhikam rocate.
variations.script: स्वतन्त्रता मह्यम् अल्पम् रोचते, किन्तु मित्रता अधिकम् रोचते।
variations.cue: Freedom appeals to me a little, but friendship much more.
variations.changed: L2-M9's alpam weakens the first half, which sharpens the contrast the second half makes

sentences.usage: How two values are ranked without either being disparaged. The first half is not withdrawn by the second; both stand, and adhikam is the whole of the ranking.

sentences.display: jīvanam hrasvam asti, ataḥ hitam eva karomi.
sentences.script: जीवनम् ह्रस्वम् अस्ति, अतः हितम् एव करोमि।
sentences.cue: Life is short, so I do only what is good.
sentences.literal: life short is, therefore the-beneficial indeed I-do

words.note: Life, a neuter noun — the whole of it rather than a lifetime or a living. It is the subject of most of this module and it takes a neuter word beside it.
L2-M3's 'short', neuter beside jīvanam. It measures a book, a vowel and a life with the same ending.
L1-M3's copula. With an 'of me' in front of it, it is the whole of 'have': mama praśnaḥ asti.
L1-M9's 'therefore'. It draws the conclusion, and the first half is what it is drawn from.
'What is good for somebody', standing here as the object of the doing. It is the module's word for a value, because mūlyam is owned as a price and stays that way.
L5-M1's emphasiser, standing AFTER the word it lifts. In front of it, it lifts nothing at all.
L1-M4's 'do' in the first person. The subject is dropped, because the -mi ending has already said who is doing it.

sentences.trap: eva stands after hitam and lifts exactly that word: I do THE GOOD and nothing else. Moved in front of hitam it would lift nothing, which is L5-M1's rule about this particle.

variations.display: jīvanam hrasvam asti, ataḥ sukham eva icchāmi.
variations.script: जीवनम् ह्रस्वम् अस्ति, अतः सुखम् एव इच्छामि।
variations.cue: Life is short, so all I want is happiness.
variations.changed: a different conclusion off the same premise, and a rather less admirable one

variations.display: jīvanam hrasvam asti, ataḥ hitam eva kartavyam.
variations.script: जीवनम् ह्रस्वम् अस्ति, अतः हितम् एव कर्तव्यम्।
variations.cue: Life is short, so what is good is what must be done.
variations.changed: L4-M1's gerundive replaces the first-person verb, which turns a personal resolve into a general obligation

variations.display: kim jīvanam hrasvam asti?
variations.script: किम् जीवनम् ह्रस्वम् अस्ति?
variations.cue: Is life short?
variations.changed: the premise asked rather than granted, which is where an argument about it would start

sentences.usage: A values claim built entirely out of words the ladder already owned, and that is the point: mūlyam is L1-M8's price and is not pressed into the moral sense, so hitam does the whole job here and in every other sentence of this module that needs it.

sentences.cue: In my view knowledge itself is freedom.

words.note: L1-M1's 'of me'. In mama mate it owns the opinion; everywhere else in this module it owns the question.
L4-M4's 'opinion' in its 'in' shape. mama mate is the whole idiom and it is how a claim about anything large is marked as a claim.
L5-M3's knowledge, neuter. It is equated here with a feminine noun, and the equation is none the worse for it: two nouns need not share a gender to be the same thing.
L5-M1's emphasiser, standing AFTER the word it lifts. In front of it, it lifts nothing at all.
Freedom, built with the same -tā suffix and feminine like every -tā word. It is a quality made into a thing, which is all the suffix ever does.

sentences.trap: Neither noun is an adjective, so neither has to agree with the other. A neuter subject and a feminine predicate is an ordinary Sanskrit equation and the verbless present carries it.

variations.display: mama mate jñānam eva mahattvam.
variations.script: मम मते ज्ञानम् एव महत्त्वम्।
variations.cue: In my view knowledge itself is greatness.
variations.changed: the neuter abstract takes the predicate slot, so subject and predicate now agree in gender as well

variations.display: mama mate svatantratā eva jñānam.
variations.script: मम मते स्वतन्त्रता एव ज्ञानम्।
variations.cue: In my view freedom itself is knowledge.
variations.changed: the equation is turned around, and eva moves with the word it lifts rather than staying put

variations.display: jñānam eva svatantratā iti aham manye.
variations.script: ज्ञानम् एव स्वतन्त्रता इति अहम् मन्ये।
variations.cue: I think knowledge itself is freedom.
variations.changed: manye and iti replace mama mate, which is the same hedge built out of a verb instead of a noun

sentences.usage: The module's largest claim and its shortest sentence, which is usually how it goes. mama mate is what keeps it a view; without it the line would be a slogan.
sentences.mnemonic: Two nouns, no verb, one claim.

sentences.display: jīvanam kim asti iti aham na jānāmi, kintu mitratā mahyam rocate.
sentences.script: जीवनम् किम् अस्ति इति अहम् न जानामि, किन्तु मित्रता मह्यम् रोचते।
sentences.cue: I do not know what life is, but I value friendship.
sentences.literal: life what is thus I not I-know, but friendship to-me is-pleasing

words.note: Life, a neuter noun — the whole of it rather than a lifetime or a living. It is the subject of most of this module and it takes a neuter word beside it.
'What' again, standing where the answer would stand. Inside iti it is a whole question rather than a question being asked.
L1-M3's copula. With an 'of me' in front of it, it is the whole of 'have': mama praśnaḥ asti.
L3-M5's quotative. It is what carries a whole question or claim into a sentence as a single thing instead of interrupting it.
'I', and the sentence turns on it: the first half is about what the speaker does not have and the second about what they do.
The negation in front of jānāmi. It denies the knowing and not the question.
'I know' in the first person, which is the shape its row is displayed in and the shape this sentence needs.
'But', and it is carrying the weight of the whole module: the big question is unanswered and something smaller is not.
Friendship. It is built from L2-M2's mitram with the -tā suffix and it is its OWN word, not a shape of it: the friend is neuter, the friendship is feminine.
L1-M1's 'to me'. rocate answers to the thing liked and never to the liker, so the person always stands in this shape.
L1-M1's 'is pleasing'. With an abstract noun in front of it, it is the ordinary way this course says a person values something.

sentences.trap: iti closes the question and na denies the knowing, and the two are easy to run together. What is negated is jānāmi alone — the question itself is not being refused.
sentences.sound: JEE-va-nam KIM AS-ti i-ti a-HAM na jaa-NAA-mi, KIN-tu mi-tra-TAA MAH-yam ROH-cha-tay. jānāmi opens on a plain j, while jñānam — the word L5-M3 built its first observation on — opens on the jñ cluster; same root, two very different openings. Said at speed iti aham runs on as ityaham.

variations.display: jīvanam kim asti iti aham na jānāmi, kintu svatantratā mahyam rocate.
variations.script: जीवनम् किम् अस्ति इति अहम् न जानामि, किन्तु स्वतन्त्रता मह्यम् रोचते।
variations.cue: I do not know what life is, but I value freedom.
variations.changed: the other abstract closes the line, and the shape of the admission does not change

variations.display: jīvanam kim asti iti aham na jānāmi.
variations.script: जीवनम् किम् अस्ति इति अहम् न जानामि।
variations.cue: I do not know what life is.
variations.changed: the affirming half falls away, leaving an admission with nothing standing beside it

variations.display: jīvanam kim asti iti aham na jānāmi, tathāpi aham santuṣṭaḥ.
variations.script: जीवनम् किम् अस्ति इति अहम् न जानामि, तथापि अहम् सन्तुष्टः।
variations.cue: I do not know what life is, and even so I am content.
variations.changed: tathāpi replaces kintu, so the second half concedes the not-knowing instead of arguing past it

mistake.display: jīvanam kim asti iti aham na jānāti, kintu mitratā mahyam rocate.
mistake.why: aham takes jānāmi and never jānāti. The -ti ending belongs to somebody else, and with aham in front of it the line has a first-person subject and a third-person verb.

sentences.usage: The module's closing posture and the honest one for a level that asks big questions: the largest of them is left open and a smaller thing is affirmed beside it. Both halves are built from the frames the module opened in S01 and S02.
sentences.mnemonic: Leave the big one open; affirm the small one.

comprehensionPool.cue: In my view what does good is what is best.
Greatness does not appeal to me.

comprehensionPool.display: mama viśvāsaḥ asti, kintu mama praśnaḥ api asti.
comprehensionPool.script: मम विश्वासः अस्ति, किन्तु मम प्रश्नः अपि अस्ति।
comprehensionPool.cue: I have a belief, but I have a question too.
I think knowledge itself is freedom.

comprehensionPool.display: kadācit jīvanam duḥkham asti, tathāpi sukham asti.
comprehensionPool.script: कदाचित् जीवनम् दुःखम् अस्ति, तथापि सुखम् अस्ति।
comprehensionPool.cue: Sometimes life is sorrow; even so there is happiness.
There is freedom, so I am content.
